How to read this page

This page scores every company in the universe on three things and highlights the few that pass every check. It is generated by six dashboard from the local data store and works offline.

Header

When the data is from (latest price date), how old the latest annual statements are, how many companies are in each branch, and the result of the last six refresh, including any failures.

Filters

Narrow everything on the Dashboard tab: by index (SMI, SMIM or other), peer group, branch, liquid shares only, AI-crash hedge candidates only (the AI hedge switch, see "AI-crash hedge" below), hiding companies with missing scores, or a ticker/name search. Filters change what you see, never the scores.

Shortlists

Two lists of companies that pass every rule (see "Shortlists and history" below). Each row shows the three scores and the two strongest reasons. A new badge marks companies that joined since the previous run; "since" shows how long a company has been on the list. "Dropped since last run" lists companies that left, with the rule they now fail.

All companies

Every company with its scores. Click a column header to sort. The small coloured number after a score is its change since the previous run. "Mom 12-1" is the share-price return from a year ago to a month ago; "% of 52w high" compares today's price with its highest price of the past year. Coloured dots are warning flags (red keeps a company off the shortlists; hover a dot for details). Click a row to open the company panel.

Company panel

  1. Scores and whether the company is on each list, or the rule it fails.
  2. Why: the metrics that push the scores up (green) or down (red).
  3. Metric breakdown: each metric's value, its percentile among peers and in its branch, the blended percentile used in the score, and its weight. Missing metrics show why they are missing.
  4. Own history: today's main valuation multiple against its value at recent fiscal-year ends. Context only, not part of the score.
  5. Price: five years of weekly prices adjusted for dividends, the 52-week range (shaded).
  6. Market risk: beta and alpha against the Swiss market (see "Beta and alpha").
  7. AI exposure: how the share moves with the AI basket, how it did in the basket's worst weeks and in named AI sell-offs, and whether it passes the AI hedge switch (see "AI-crash hedge").
  8. Flags with explanations.
  9. Key financials: up to four fiscal years in the reporting currency, with CHF below when the company reports in USD or EUR.
  10. Peers: the company against the median of its peer group on five key metrics.

The three scores

Value asks how cheap the company is relative to what it earns, owns and pays out. Quality asks how profitable, cash-generative and financially sound it is. Growth asks how steadily revenue, profits and cash flow have grown. Each score runs from 0 (worst in its comparison group) to 100 (best).

  1. Every metric is ranked as a percentile within the company's branch (general, financials, real estate) and within its peer group.
  2. The two percentiles are blended, giving small peer groups less weight.
  3. A score is the weighted average of its metrics' blended percentiles, using only the metrics available for that company.
  4. If too few metrics are available, the score shows "insufficient data" instead of a number.
Formulas

Percentile: companies with a value are ranked from worst to best; percentile = (rank − 1) ÷ (count − 1) × 100. Ties share the average rank, and a company alone in its group gets 50. Metrics where lower is better are ranked in reverse. Extremes, such as an enterprise value ≤ 0, rank as best or worst as described in the glossary.

Blending: blended = w × peer percentile + (1 − w) × branch percentile, with w = n ÷ (n + ), where n is the number of peers with a value. A peer group of 62 counts about 89%, a group of 5 about 38%.

Score: Σ(weight × blended percentile) ÷ Σ(weights of the available metrics). Minimum metrics: Value , Quality , Growth .

Branches and peer groups

Banks, insurers and property companies can't be judged on the same metrics as an industrial company: a bank's borrowing is its business, and a property company's accounts are dominated by property valuations. So each company sits in a branch, which decides which metrics apply, and in a peer group built from SIX's industry sectors, which decides who it is compared with.

Metric glossary

Every metric used in a score: what it means, how it is computed from the annual statements (using Yahoo's line-item names), whether higher or lower is better, and where it is used with its weight.

Momentum and liquidity

Momentum 12-1 is the dividend-adjusted share-price return from 12 months ago to 1 month ago; the last month is skipped because very recent moves tend to reverse. It needs about 13 months of prices. It is not part of the scores but guards the shortlists: research shows that cheap stocks which keep falling often keep falling.

% of 52-week high is today's close divided by the highest close of the last 252 trading days. A falling knife is a company in the bottom of the universe on momentum that also trades below of its 52-week high.

Liquidity is the median daily value traded over the last three months. Below CHF a share is flagged as thinly traded, and below CHF market cap it is a micro cap. Both keep a company off the shortlists, because its price may move a lot when you buy or sell.

Beta and alpha

Both compare a share with the Swiss market, measured by the SPI (Swiss Performance Index, dividends included), using weekly returns over the last weeks (about three years). A share needs at least weekly returns, otherwise no numbers are shown.

Beta answers "how risky is it compared with the market?": 1.3 means the share typically moves 30% more than the market, 0.6 that it is calmer. Alpha answers "did it beat the market?": the yearly return beyond what its beta alone would have earned (risk-free rate taken as zero; Swiss short rates were about 1% or less, so the error is small). Alpha describes the past, not the future.

When the market explains little of a share's moves (R² below ), the panel says so: beta is then only a rough guide. Thinly traded shares often look calm simply because their price rarely updates, and tiny ones jump around: for shares flagged thin_trading or micro_cap the market columns are greyed and sort below the rest. A price that never moved shows no numbers. Beta and alpha are information only: they change no score, list or flag.

AI-crash hedge

How each share moves with a basket of US AI stocks: , equally weighted (so the biggest names don't dominate) and converted to Swiss francs, because that is what a Swiss investor feels. Weekly returns are used because SIX closes hours before the US market.

The panel shows the correlation with the basket, the AI-specific sensitivity (how much the share moves with the basket beyond what the Swiss market explains), the share's average return in the basket's worst of weeks next to the SPI's, and its returns in named AI sell-offs (peak to trough of the basket).

The AI hedge switch keeps only companies that pass every rule: at least weekly returns; AI correlation ≤ and AI-specific sensitivity ≤ ; in the basket's worst weeks an average return of at least zero, or a loss of at most of the SPI's; Quality ≥ and Value ≥ ; no red flag, liquid. It narrows the table and both shortlists; it changes no score.

Caveats: correlations tend to rise in a crash, so past calm is no guarantee; three years is one market period; and thinly traded shares look calm because their price rarely moves (they are excluded by the liquidity rule).

Analyst estimates

Under the scores, each company shows how analysts' earnings-per-share estimate for the current fiscal year (the next year when there is none) changed over the last 90 days, and how many analysts raised or cut it in the last 30 days. The "Est. 90d" column in the table holds the same change. The figures come from Yahoo Finance and are refreshed daily; companies without analyst coverage show "No analyst estimates".

Estimates are not part of the scores. They work like momentum: when analysts are clearly cutting (a fall of or more with more cuts than raises) the company gets an amber estimates_falling flag and is kept off the Growth at a reasonable price list, because that list is a bet on growth expectations. The Value with quality list only shows the warning.

News

Each company panel lists headlines from the last 90 days before the data date, found by searching Google News (Swiss German and French editions) for the company's name. Claude reads each headline once, decides whether it is really about the company (not a namesake or a street) and tags it: warning (losses or profit warning, guidance cut, legal or regulatory trouble, management exit, restructuring or asset sale, capital increase, accounting or auditor issue, delisting, takeover or merger), positive (guidance raise, buyback or dividend, contract or order win) or neutral. Headlines that are not about the company are hidden, as are headlines not yet checked.

A warning headline from the last days raises the amber news_warning flag; older ones stay in the list but no longer raise it. It is information only: it never takes a company off a shortlist, and the tags are machine-made and can be wrong, so open the article before acting on it.

Warning flags

Red flags keep a company off the shortlists; amber flags are information.

Shortlists and history

Value with quality: Value ≥ and Quality ≥ , no red flag, liquid. Cheap alone isn't enough: cheap companies that are also sound have historically done much better than cheap companies in trouble ("value traps"). Ordered by Value + ½ × Quality.

Growth at a reasonable price: Growth ≥ , Quality ≥ , Value ≥ , growth consistency ≥ , positive 12-1 momentum, share dilution ≤ , no red flag except falling knife, liquid. The Value floor stops this list from filling up with expensive favourites. Ordered by Growth + ½ × Quality.

The Dashboard shows the top of each list. Every run saves the day's scores in data/screener/, and the page compares them with the previous saved run: new marks companies that joined a list, "dropped" lists those that left with the rule they now fail, "since" is the first day of the current unbroken stay on the list, and the small numbers in the table are score changes.

Top 5 portfolio

The card at the top of the Dashboard answers "which five to buy, and how much of each". There are two versions: Best overall picks from both shortlists; AI-crash hedge picks from the companies that pass the AI hedge switch (see "AI-crash hedge"). A candidate also needs weekly returns, a price in CHF and a median daily turnover of at least CHF (twice the thin-trading line, so stale prices don't pass for calm ones).

  1. Score of a stock: the average of its Value, Quality and Growth scores (a missing Growth score counts as 50).
  2. Moving together: the correlation of weekly returns between every pair of candidates over the last three years. Five stocks that rise and fall together are less safe than five that don't.
  3. The choice: every group of candidates is scored as average score − × 100 × average correlation, with at most from one peer group, and the best group wins.
  4. How much of each: the money is split so that each stock carries the same share of the group's risk: calmer stocks get more. Each weight stays between and and is rounded to steps.
  5. Buy and hold: the five only change when one leaves its pool (the replacement takes over its weight and the others keep theirs) or when a new group scores at least points higher (then all weights are recomputed). The card says since when the five have been unchanged and lists every change with its reason.

Type an amount to see how many whole shares of each stock it buys at the latest closing price and how much cash is left. The amount stays in this browser only.

Caveats: three years is one market period; correlations tend to rise in a crash; this is a choice by fixed rules from past prices and today's scores, not a forecast and not investment advice.

Your portfolio

The panel beside the top-five card follows the portfolio actually bought, as saved in the project's holdings.toml file: one entry per purchase, with the stock, the day it was bought, the amount in CHF and, once sold, the day it was sold. The amounts are assumed.

  1. Buy and sell prices: a purchase is made at the price per share recorded for it (for example the opening price, for a purchase made in the morning) or, if none is recorded, at that day's closing price, or the next trading day's if the market was shut; a sale is made at the closing price. A purchase with a recorded price is compared with the SMI at its opening level that day. Shares are kept as fractions, so the amount is exactly what went in.
  2. Cash and new money: money from a sale stays in the portfolio as cash and pays for the next purchase first. Only the part that cash does not cover counts as new money; invested is all new money so far, less any money taken out.
  3. Gain: value now minus invested, in CHF and as a percentage of invested. Selling one stock and buying another never changes the gain by itself.
  4. Against the SMI: the grey line puts the same new money into the SMI on the same days (and takes it out when money is taken out). Its percentage is worked out the same way, so the two numbers compare like for like.
  5. Price-only: dividends are left out of both the stocks and the SMI (the SMI is a price index), so the comparison stays fair but both understate the total return.
  6. No price: if a stock stops getting prices (it left the universe or was taken over) it stays in at its last closing price, marked "no price since".

Trying a change: Edit lets you change stocks, dates, amounts and buy prices (leave the price empty for the closing price), add or remove rows; everything recalculates at once. The change is a draft kept in this browser only, marked "Draft — not saved". Back to saved throws it away. Copy for saving copies it as holdings.toml text: send it to whoever keeps the file, or paste it into the file, and it appears on every copy of the page after the next build.

Readjustment

When the names your portfolio holds differ from the five the card picks, the Readjustment panel under the card prices the switch at today's closing prices: what to sell, what to buy, and what each sale locks in.

  1. Held beside picked: in the card, each picked name is marked kept (already held) or new (not held); names held but no longer picked are listed under the five as dropped, with the reason from the change list. The held names follow the Your portfolio panel: while a draft exists, the draft.
  2. The money: everything is valued at the latest close: the held stocks, cash from earlier sales and any new money typed in. Each picked name gets its weight of that total; the difference to what is held becomes a sale, a trim, a top-up or a buy in whole shares. A top-up or trim smaller than CHF or than one share is left as is. If the buys cost more than the money available, the plan says how much more is needed rather than cutting them.
  3. What a sale locks in: the sale value minus what was paid for those shares (pro rata for a trim). "Locks in" adds this up: a gain or loss made real today, before fees, stamp duty and taxes, which are not counted. A name without a current price is listed at its last close and left out of this total.
  4. Weights: Suggested uses the card's weights, Equal the same amount in each, Custom lets you type a weight or a franc amount per name; if custom weights don't add up to 100% the plan says so and uses them as typed. These choices stay in this browser only.
  5. Apply to draft turns the plan into a draft of Your portfolio: sold names end today, trimmed lots are split, buys become new lots at today's close. Nothing is saved until the draft is copied into the holdings file.

The plan at the suggested weights is saved with every build (data/advice/), so the advice to switch can be judged later.

Track record

The Track record section judges every five the model ever proposed, so the advice can be checked against what then happened.

  1. A proposed five is one version's five names with their weights, from the first day they were shown. Every change of names or weights starts a new entry; replaced entries stay in the table, so the record never drops its misses.
  2. Bought and held: each five is valued as if bought at the closing prices of the day it was proposed, at its weights, and held with no changes. The reader sees the page in the evening and can act the next morning, so this is kind to the model by one overnight move.
  3. Marks: the return after 1 week, 1 month, 3, 6 and 12 months (, , , and calendar days, at the first close on or after) and to date, each against the SMI over the same stretch; the lead is the difference. A mark not reached yet shows "–"; nothing is invented. A tick marks a five that is ahead of the SMI to date.
  4. His portfolio: the same marks for the portfolio actually bought, counted from the first purchase and taken from the Your portfolio line (prices paid, later changes, cash and money taken out included), so "did the advice pay" sits next to "was the advice good".
  5. Price-only, like everything on this page: dividends are left out on both sides. One week or one month says little; the record becomes meaningful over years.

Data and caveats

  • Prices, annual statements and ratios come from Yahoo Finance (unofficial, personal use; the data can contain errors).
  • A fiscal year is used only months after it ends, when annual reports are out. Only annual statements are used, so figures can be more than a year old; the panel shows the statement date.
  • All price-based metrics are in CHF. Companies reporting in USD or EUR are converted: balance-sheet items at the rate on the period end, flows at the average rate of that year. Growth rates use the reporting currency, so currency moves don't count as growth.
  • Earnings mean income from continuing operations, so a gain from selling or spinning off a business doesn't make a company look cheap.
  • Only about four years of statements are available, so growth rates and stability measures rest on few data points. Recent listings have shorter histories.
  • Scores are relative: a high Value score means cheap compared with peers today, not cheap in absolute terms.
  • These are metrics for personal research, not investment advice.
